name: 2,000 stations, large capacities
expr: (lambda r: [r[0], flow_check(args[0], args[1], list(r[1]), args[2], args[3])])(flow_plan(args[0], list(args[1]), args[2], args[3]))
show: 2,000 stations, 10,000 random lines, capacities up to 1,000,000
why: Paths found by depth-first search are long, and their smallest capacity is usually small, so that method sends a little at a time, for hours. Shortest paths (Edmonds-Karp) need at most V · E / 2 rounds whatever the capacities.

name: 160 layers of 30
expr: (lambda r: [r[0], flow_check(args[0], args[1], list(r[1]), args[2], args[3])])(flow_plan(args[0], list(args[1]), args[2], args[3]))
show: 4,802 stations in 160 layers of 30, three lines from each station to the next layer
why: Every path from the source to the sink is about 160 lines long. Edmonds-Karp runs one breadth-first search per path, and there are thousands of paths: about 13 seconds even in desktop Python, longer in the browser. Dinic finds all the shortest paths of one length in one phase, with one search and pointers that never go back (lesson 3).
